name: castle portcullis gate set in the wall
label: beodeul_dungeon/earth.portcullis

surfaces.part: stone wall section with gate opening
portcullis spikes at top of opening

answer.evidence: The whole 48x32 sprite is a flat front-facing wall with a dark arched gate opening and portcullis spikes at the top (rows 4-8). The wall is brick or stone texture seen face-on (column scan: lightness steady at 86-119 for rows 1-5, then dark 41-45 for rows 4-24 inside the opening). Row 0 is a light 1-row coping line, which counts as a rim. A narrow sill at rows 29-30 has a lighter line at row 29 but is only 1-2 rows. No horizontal surface is visible with depth. As a wall-mounted piece it is flat by design and reads as front elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a stone wall frame with a dark portcullis opening. The stone blocks show some per-block shading and speckle, and the gate interior has spikes and bars. The measured facts are 11 visible tones per tile, 7% near-flat coverage and 21% neutral dark edge pixels. That is comparable to the hedge (9 tones) and below the well (20) and stall (17). Its flat coverage is under the stall's 13%. The stone ramp has about 4 steps (light highlight, mid grey, dark grey, deep). The references use 5-6. The dark gate interior is a large near-black area with little variation beyond the spikes and a few lighter dots, so it reads somewhat flat. Outlines are mixed: the dark edges lean a little neutral and are less clearly tinted than the references' material-tone outlines. Overall it is a competent piece but a bit thinner in shading depth and tint than the Beodeul props, so it is not clearly at the reference level.

surfaces.part: stone wall frame with portcullis opening

answer.evidence: The object is a flat wall-mounted gate drawn face-on: a stone wall section 48px wide with a dark opening, spikes along the top and a low threshold. The only top-like element is a 1-row light coping line at row 0, which is an outline-style edge and not a top surface. The wall and gate are vertical faces, and no receding side face is shown. Rows 26-29 form a small threshold step, but it is thin and not the main body. For a wall_mounted kind this flat elevation is plausible, so it is measured as front_elevation with no main top.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a stone gate arch with a portcullis, the same kind as the references (a standing prop). Measured facts: 11 visible tones per 16x16 tile, which is above prop-hedge (9) and below stall-cheese (17) and well-roofed (20). Near-flat coverage is 7%, so there are no large flat fills; stall-cheese is at 13%. Only 21% of dark edge pixels are near-neutral, so the outlines lean toward the tint of the neighbouring stone and are not a uniform black sticker line. By eye, the stone blocks are shaded individually with highlight, mid and dark faces, which gives about 4 steps on the stone ramp. The dark portcullis interior carries bars and spikes with some variation. The total palette is small (14 colours), so the shading is slightly shallower than the best references. The piece is still a coherent, textured prop that would sit acceptably next to the hedge and bench.

answer.evidence: This is a flat front view of a stone wall with an arched gate opening. The only light rows at the top are a 1-row coping line at row 0 (x=12 and x=24 L=197) and a short band in rows 1-3 that fades to the wall colour, which counts as a rim and not a top surface. The portcullis spikes in rows 4-8 and the dark opening in rows 4-24 are vertical faces. Rows 25-29 show a few stepped horizontal bands with a light line at row 29, but they are 1-2 row strips and do not form a foreshortened top plane. The silhouette is a constant 48 wide for all 32 rows, with no side face and no ellipse. Because it is wall-mounted and meant to be flat, it reads as front elevation.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a stone arch with a spiked portcullis. The stone blocks are shaded one by one with a light top edge, mid face, dark joint and dark rim, which gives about 5 steps. The dark interior carries speckle and shows some variation. The portcullis bars are the shallowest part, with about 3 tones. Only 21% of the dark edge pixels are neutral, so the outlines lean toward the tint of the neighbouring stone instead of forming a black sticker line. Visible tones per tile are 11, which is in line with the hedge (9) and below the stall (17) and well (20). Near-flat coverage is 7%, in the range of the stall (13%) and well below the limit for a flat fill. It is slightly thinner than the best references, mainly in the portcullis, but a careful artist would accept it beside them.

surfaces.part: wall coping strip along the top
stone wall facade with the arched gate opening, spikes and dark interior

answer.evidence: This is a flat face-on wall panel. The wall is a 1-row light coping line at row 0, with no front-edge line and no eave shadow below it, so it counts as a rim and not a top surface. The gate opening is a dark rectangle with spike tips at rows 4-8, and its frame, wall stones and sill are all vertical faces. The grey bands at rows 21-27 inside the opening read as bars or a step seen face-on, not as a horizontal top. The silhouette is a constant 48 px wide on every row, so there is no ellipse and no receding side face. Wall-mounted pieces may be flat, but there is no top surface.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a stone arch with a dark portcullis interior and spikes. Measured facts: 11 visible tones per tile, 7% near-flat coverage, 21% neutral dark edge pixels. That is comparable to prop-hedge (9) but below the well (20) and stall (17). The stone blocks show a few grey steps (highlight, mid, dark) and some per-block variation, but the stone ramp is closer to 3-4 steps than the 5-6 on the references. The portcullis interior is a dark mass with sparse bars and little internal texture, and it reads as a mostly flat dark fill. The outline is mostly dark grey-blue stone tone, so it is not a hard black sticker line, though some edges lean neutral. Overall it is competent and not sticker-like, but it is thinner and flatter than the richer references (well, stall) at the same scale, and the portcullis grille lacks the shading, rivet and wood-grain detail Beodeul would give it. When in doubt, fail.
